    "id": "dsid_cd133e76dd62456d9182217e280e2cb3",
    "path": "/knowledge/company/sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/coding-standards/concurrency-primitives-and-affinity-guidelines-2026.json",

    "source": "EnterpriseRAG/confluence",
    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"concurrency-primitives-and-affinity-guidelines-2026\",\n  \"space\": \"architecture-and-standards/coding-standards\",\n  \"author\": \"Ava Chen\",\n  \"owner_team\": \"engineering\",\n  \"status\": \"published\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-01-10\",\n  \"last_updated\": \"2026-03-04\",\n  \"reviewers\": [\n    \"Diego Morales\",\n    \"Priya Nair\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"concurrency\",\n    \"runtime\",\n    \"cpu-affinity\",\n    \"gpu-affinity\",\n    \"best-practices\"\n  ],\n  \"related_pages\": [\n    \"/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/sequence-length-aware-kernel-selection-guidelines-2026\",\n    \"/confluence/architecture-and-standards/infra-standards/graceful-gpu-preemption-and-prewarming-guidelines-2026\"\n  ],\n  \"confidentiality\": \"internal\",\n  \"content\": \"Overview\\\\n\\\\nThis document defines recommended concurrency primitives, thread/actor affinity patterns, and safe integration points for Redwood's inference runtime and associated services. The goal is to reduce latency variability, avoid priority inversion on shared GPU/CPU resources, and make component-level behavior predictable under both steady-state and burst loads.\\\\n\\\\nAudience\\\\n- Runtime engineers\\\\n- Infra and SRE teams\\\\n- SDK and client-library maintainers\\\\n\\\\nGoals\\\\n- Provide low-friction, testable concurrency patterns that limit tail-latency impact on multi-tenant GPU hosts.\\\\n- Standardize affinity approaches across CPU-bound pre/post processing, scheduler threads, and GPU work submission paths.\\\\n- Give clear migration guidance away from ad-hoc locking and blocking I/O in hot paths.\\\\n\\\\nScope\\\\nThis guideline covers:\\\\n- Inference serving processes (request dispatch, KV cache, batching)\\\\n- Pre/post-processing workers and tokenization pipelines\\\\n- Client SDKs that perform local batching or streaming\\\\nNot in scope: language-level runtime internals (language VM implementation details).\\\\n\\\\nPrinciples\\\\n1. Prefer non-blocking coordination in hot paths: use lock-free queues, atomics, and single-producer-single-consumer (SPSC) rings where possible.\\\\n2. Isolate blocking work into bounded, observable worker pools with backpressure signals.\\\\n3. Bind critical threads to stable CPU sets and avoid OS-level preemption during GPU submission windows.\\\\n4. Make affinity and scheduling observable: expose metrics for queue lengths, thread utilization, and preemption events.\\\\n\\\\nRecommended primitives by component\\\\n(Use the table below to pick the right primitive for each component)\\\\n\\\\nComponent | Recommended Primitive | Rationale | Max concurrency\\\\n---|---:|---|---:\\\\nRequest dispatch / ingress thread | SPSC ring buffer + atomic cursor | Minimizes allocation and lock overhead; predictable latency | 1 per ingress socket\\\\nKV cache access (read-dominant) | Seqlock or RCU-style snapshot | Readers fast; writers do rare consistent updates | many readers, few writers\\\\nKV cache writes / metadata updates | Mutex + short critical section OR per-shard lock striping | Keep write windows short to avoid contention | #shards == CPU sockets\\\\nBatch assembly | Lock-free queue with batch-coalescer thread | Allows continuous enqueuing while a single consumer creates batches | bounded pool of batchers (2\\u20134)\\\\nBlocking I/O (logs, metrics flush) | Asynchronous worker pool with bounded queue and QoS | Prevents blocking hot threads; degrade QoS under overload | configurable, default 8\\\\nTelemetry enrichment | Per-request pre-allocated buffer + atomic append | Avoid heap allocation in fast path | per-thread buffer\\\\n\\\\nAffinity guidelines\\\\n- CPU affinity: bind the following to dedicated core sets where supported by the host OS/hypervisor:\\\\n  - GPU submission threads: isolate on a small core set with real-time bias if available.\\\\n  - Batch coalescer / KV eviction threads: colocate with NUMA-local cores to reduce remote memory access.\\\\n  - Tokenizer and detokenizer pools: keep within the same NUMA domain as the dispatcher when latency is critical.\\\\n- GPU affinity: prefer single-GPU submission per process when using model shards that maintain an in-GPU KV cache. For multi-GPU processes, pin submission threads to the GPU's preferred CPU set to reduce PCIe context switch costs.\\\\n- Avoid oversubscription: ensure sum(allocated_cpu_shares) <= node_cpu_capacity - reserved_system_cores. We recommend reserving at least 1 full core per GPU for submission and poll loops.\\\\n\\\\nThread pool sizing heuristics\\\\n1. Hot path/poller threads: 1 thread per hardware queue (do not use threadpool for pollers).\\\\n2. CPU-bound workers (tokenizers): min(2 * hardware_threads_local, 8) with aggressive cooperative yielding.\\\\n3. Blocking work pools: small bounded pools (4\\u201316) with adaptive throttling based on queue latency and SLO signals.\\\\n\\\\nBackpressure and QoS\\\\n- All public enqueue points must return an overload signal within 20ms when internal queues are above their configured high-water mark. Implementations MUST provide both:\\\\n  1) an explicit API error (e.g., 429 / X-Queue-State header)\\\\n  2) a telemetry signal (metered count of rejected requests)\\\\n- For SDK-local batching, prefer a hybrid policy: wait up to 15ms or until batch_size threshold, whichever comes first. Expose a hook to bypass batching for latency-sensitive calls.\\\\n\\\\nInteraction patterns and safe APIs\\\\n- Provide a single \\\"submission fence\\\" API for GPU work that:\\\\n  - returns quickly after queuing to kernel (non-blocking where supported)\\\\n  - exposes a future/promise for completion so higher layers can await if necessary\\\\n- Expose cancellation tokens for in-flight requests. Cancellation must be cooperative: threads should check token at known yield points (e.g., between tokenizer stages, before batch add).\\\\n\\\\nTesting and validation\\\\n1. Microbenchmarks: Every change to a hot-path primitive must include a microbenchmark that measures median and 99.9th percentile latency under realistic contention (>= 8 concurrent clients).\\\\n2. Fault-injection: Synthesize preemption and core-steal scenarios in CI (containerized fault injection) to validate graceful degradation.\\\\n3. Nightly stress: Run an open-loop stress test that simulates burst patterns and validates queue high-water eviction behaves as expected.\\\\n\\\\nOperational runbook (short)\\\\n1. Symptom: rising 99.9th percentile latency with stable median.\\\\n  - Check: batcher queue length, KV cache writer queue, CPU steal and RCU retry counters.\\\\n  - Mitigation: temporarily increase batcher count (if space allows) or scale horizontally to relieve co-located CPU pressure.\\\\n2. Symptom: CPU-level preemption spikes during GPU submission window.\\\\n  - Check: kernel-level SCHED_LOG or cgroup throttling metrics.\\\\n  - Mitigation: move submission threads to reserved cores; enable prewarm submission path.\\\\n\\\\nMigration checklist (for teams moving from coarse locking)\\\\n- Identify hot lock holders via p99 profiling (perf/async-profiler).\\\\n- Introduce SPSC ring or atomic fast-path with fallback lock for complex updates.\\\\n- Add metrics for fast-path vs fallback-path counts.\\\\n- Gradually flip traffic with canary (5%, 25%, 100%) while monitoring tail-latency and rejection rates.\\\\n\\\\nExample patterns\\\\n- SPSC ring producer pseudocode:\\\\n```\\\\nclass SpscRing {\\\\n  atomic<uint64_t> head;\\\\n  atomic<uint64_t> tail;\\\\n  Item buffer[N];\\\\n\\\\n  bool push(Item x) {\\\\n    auto h = head.load();\\\\n    if ((h - tail.load()) >= N) return false; // full\\\\n    buffer[h % N] = x;\\\\n    head.store(h + 1);\\\\n    return true;\\\\n  }\\\\n}\\\\n```\\\\n- Bounded async worker pool (CLI): configure via env vars: WORKER_POOL_SIZE=8, WORKER_QUEUE_MAX=1024, WORKER_QOS=low\\\\n\\\\nOwnership and compliance\\\\n- Runtime-serving: owning team = eng-serving-runtime\\\\n- SDK batching: owning team = eng-developer-experience\\\\n- Enforcement: code review checklist item \\\"concurrency primitive justification\\\" must be present for PRs touching hot-paths.\\\\n\\\\nMetrics to emit (minimum)\\\\n- queue.length.{component} (gauge)\\\\n- queue.rejects.{component} (counter)\\\\n- thread.preemptions.{thread_group} (counter)\\\\n- cpu.affinity.migrations (counter)\\\\n- batch.size.histogram (histogram)\\\\n\\\\nReferences and related pages\\\\n- See: runtime hot-path profiling playbook and kernel scheduling guidance in eng-serving-runtime.\\\\n\\\\nAppendix: Decision rationale\\\\nTeams repeatedly observed that coarse-grained mutexes introduced p99 amplification when a single slow writer blocked many readers during model warmup and KV updates. We decided to favor reader-fast patterns and bounded worker pools to create predictable overload behavior and simpler operational signals.\\\\n\\\\nDocument history\\\\n- 2026-01-10: Drafted by Ava Chen\\\\n- 2026-02-08: Reviewed by Diego Morales and Priya Nair; added affinity heuristics\\\\n- 2026-03-04: Published (this version)\\\\n\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"content\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_cd133e76dd62456d9182217e280e2cb3\"\n}",

{
  "title": "concurrency-primitives-and-affinity-guidelines-2026",
  "space": "architecture-and-standards/coding-standards",
  "author": "Ava Chen",
  "owner_team": "engineering",
  "status": "published",
  "created_at": "2026-01-10",
  "last_updated": "2026-03-04",
  "reviewers": [
    "Diego Morales",
    "Priya Nair"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "concurrency",
    "runtime",
    "cpu-affinity",
    "gpu-affinity",
    "best-practices"
  ],
  "related_pages": [
    "/confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/sequence-length-aware-kernel-selection-guidelines-2026",
    "/confluence/architecture-and-standards/infra-standards/graceful-gpu-preemption-and-prewarming-guidelines-2026"
  ],
  "confidentiality": "internal",
  "content": "Overview\\n\\nThis document defines recommended concurrency primitives, thread/actor affinity patterns, and safe integration points for Redwood's inference runtime and associated services. The goal is to reduce latency variability, avoid priority inversion on shared GPU/CPU resources, and make component-level behavior predictable under both steady-state and burst loads.\\n\\nAudience\\n- Runtime engineers\\n- Infra and SRE teams\\n- SDK and client-library maintainers\\n\\nGoals\\n- Provide low-friction, testable concurrency patterns that limit tail-latency impact on multi-tenant GPU hosts.\\n- Standardize affinity approaches across CPU-bound pre/post processing, scheduler threads, and GPU work submission paths.\\n- Give clear migration guidance away from ad-hoc locking and blocking I/O in hot paths.\\n\\nScope\\nThis guideline covers:\\n- Inference serving processes (request dispatch, KV cache, batching)\\n- Pre/post-processing workers and tokenization pipelines\\n- Client SDKs that perform local batching or streaming\\nNot in scope: language-level runtime internals (language VM implementation details).\\n\\nPrinciples\\n1. Prefer non-blocking coordination in hot paths: use lock-free queues, atomics, and single-producer-single-consumer (SPSC) rings where possible.\\n2. Isolate blocking work into bounded, observable worker pools with backpressure signals.\\n3. Bind critical threads to stable CPU sets and avoid OS-level preemption during GPU submission windows.\\n4. Make affinity and scheduling observable: expose metrics for queue lengths, thread utilization, and preemption events.\\n\\nRecommended primitives by component\\n(Use the table below to pick the right primitive for each component)\\n\\nComponent | Recommended Primitive | Rationale | Max concurrency\\n---|---:|---|---:\\nRequest dispatch / ingress thread | SPSC ring buffer + atomic cursor | Minimizes allocation and lock overhead; predictable latency | 1 per ingress socket\\nKV cache access (read-dominant) | Seqlock or RCU-style snapshot | Readers fast; writers do rare consistent updates | many readers, few writers\\nKV cache writes / metadata updates | Mutex + short critical section OR per-shard lock striping | Keep write windows short to avoid contention | #shards == CPU sockets\\nBatch assembly | Lock-free queue with batch-coalescer thread | Allows continuous enqueuing while a single consumer creates batches | bounded pool of batchers (2\u20134)\\nBlocking I/O (logs, metrics flush) | Asynchronous worker pool with bounded queue and QoS | Prevents blocking hot threads; degrade QoS under overload | configurable, default 8\\nTelemetry enrichment | Per-request pre-allocated buffer + atomic append | Avoid heap allocation in fast path | per-thread buffer\\n\\nAffinity guidelines\\n- CPU affinity: bind the following to dedicated core sets where supported by the host OS/hypervisor:\\n  - GPU submission threads: isolate on a small core set with real-time bias if available.\\n  - Batch coalescer / KV eviction threads: colocate with NUMA-local cores to reduce remote memory access.\\n  - Tokenizer and detokenizer pools: keep within the same NUMA domain as the dispatcher when latency is critical.\\n- GPU affinity: prefer single-GPU submission per process when using model shards that maintain an in-GPU KV cache. For multi-GPU processes, pin submission threads to the GPU's preferred CPU set to reduce PCIe context switch costs.\\n- Avoid oversubscription: ensure sum(allocated_cpu_shares) <= node_cpu_capacity - reserved_system_cores. We recommend reserving at least 1 full core per GPU for submission and poll loops.\\n\\nThread pool sizing heuristics\\n1. Hot path/poller threads: 1 thread per hardware queue (do not use threadpool for pollers).\\n2. CPU-bound workers (tokenizers): min(2 * hardware_threads_local, 8) with aggressive cooperative yielding.\\n3. Blocking work pools: small bounded pools (4\u201316) with adaptive throttling based on queue latency and SLO signals.\\n\\nBackpressure and QoS\\n- All public enqueue points must return an overload signal within 20ms when internal queues are above their configured high-water mark. Implementations MUST provide both:\\n  1) an explicit API error (e.g., 429 / X-Queue-State header)\\n  2) a telemetry signal (metered count of rejected requests)\\n- For SDK-local batching, prefer a hybrid policy: wait up to 15ms or until batch_size threshold, whichever comes first. Expose a hook to bypass batching for latency-sensitive calls.\\n\\nInteraction patterns and safe APIs\\n- Provide a single \"submission fence\" API for GPU work that:\\n  - returns quickly after queuing to kernel (non-blocking where supported)\\n  - exposes a future/promise for completion so higher layers can await if necessary\\n- Expose cancellation tokens for in-flight requests. Cancellation must be cooperative: threads should check token at known yield points (e.g., between tokenizer stages, before batch add).\\n\\nTesting and validation\\n1. Microbenchmarks: Every change to a hot-path primitive must include a microbenchmark that measures median and 99.9th percentile latency under realistic contention (>= 8 concurrent clients).\\n2. Fault-injection: Synthesize preemption and core-steal scenarios in CI (containerized fault injection) to validate graceful degradation.\\n3. Nightly stress: Run an open-loop stress test that simulates burst patterns and validates queue high-water eviction behaves as expected.\\n\\nOperational runbook (short)\\n1. Symptom: rising 99.9th percentile latency with stable median.\\n  - Check: batcher queue length, KV cache writer queue, CPU steal and RCU retry counters.\\n  - Mitigation: temporarily increase batcher count (if space allows) or scale horizontally to relieve co-located CPU pressure.\\n2. Symptom: CPU-level preemption spikes during GPU submission window.\\n  - Check: kernel-level SCHED_LOG or cgroup throttling metrics.\\n  - Mitigation: move submission threads to reserved cores; enable prewarm submission path.\\n\\nMigration checklist (for teams moving from coarse locking)\\n- Identify hot lock holders via p99 profiling (perf/async-profiler).\\n- Introduce SPSC ring or atomic fast-path with fallback lock for complex updates.\\n- Add metrics for fast-path vs fallback-path counts.\\n- Gradually flip traffic with canary (5%, 25%, 100%) while monitoring tail-latency and rejection rates.\\n\\nExample patterns\\n- SPSC ring producer pseudocode:\\n```\\nclass SpscRing {\\n  atomic<uint64_t> head;\\n  atomic<uint64_t> tail;\\n  Item buffer[N];\\n\\n  bool push(Item x) {\\n    auto h = head.load();\\n    if ((h - tail.load()) >= N) return false; // full\\n    buffer[h % N] = x;\\n    head.store(h + 1);\\n    return true;\\n  }\\n}\\n```\\n- Bounded async worker pool (CLI): configure via env vars: WORKER_POOL_SIZE=8, WORKER_QUEUE_MAX=1024, WORKER_QOS=low\\n\\nOwnership and compliance\\n- Runtime-serving: owning team = eng-serving-runtime\\n- SDK batching: owning team = eng-developer-experience\\n- Enforcement: code review checklist item \"concurrency primitive justification\" must be present for PRs touching hot-paths.\\n\\nMetrics to emit (minimum)\\n- queue.length.{component} (gauge)\\n- queue.rejects.{component} (counter)\\n- thread.preemptions.{thread_group} (counter)\\n- cpu.affinity.migrations (counter)\\n- batch.size.histogram (histogram)\\n\\nReferences and related pages\\n- See: runtime hot-path profiling playbook and kernel scheduling guidance in eng-serving-runtime.\\n\\nAppendix: Decision rationale\\nTeams repeatedly observed that coarse-grained mutexes introduced p99 amplification when a single slow writer blocked many readers during model warmup and KV updates. We decided to favor reader-fast patterns and bounded worker pools to create predictable overload behavior and simpler operational signals.\\n\\nDocument history\\n- 2026-01-10: Drafted by Ava Chen\\n- 2026-02-08: Reviewed by Diego Morales and Priya Nair; added affinity heuristics\\n- 2026-03-04: Published (this version)\\n",

    "content": "{\n  \"title\": \"Postmortem: EU API latency and elevated 5xx (edge routing cache)\",\n  \"space\": \"oncall-and-incident-response\",\n  \"author\": \"Ava Chen\",\n  \"owner_team\": \"engineering\",\n  \"status\": \"published\",\n  \"created_at\": \"2026-01-20\",\n  \"last_updated\": \"2026-02-01\",\n  \"reviewers\": [\n    \"Elliot Price\",\n    \"Jonas Weber\"\n  ],\n  \"labels\": [\n    \"postmortem\",\n    \"sev2\",\n    \"customer-impacting\",\n    \"eng-platform\",\n    \"hosted-api\",\n    \"edge-routing\"\n  ],\n  \"confidentiality\": \"internal\",\n  \"body\": \"h1. Summary\\nOn 2026-01-19 we experienced elevated p95 latency and intermittent HTTP 5xx for a subset of EU-hosted API traffic. The incident lasted 47 minutes end-to-end. Customer impact was concentrated in the eu-west region and primarily affected chat completions with streaming enabled.\\n\\n*Customer impact:* Yes (degraded performance + partial errors)\\n*Severity:* SEV-2\\n*Owning engineering team:* Platform Engineering (Traffic & Edge)\\n*Primary services:* edge-router, request-gateway, redis-edge-cache\\n\\nh1. Impact\\n* ~12% of EU requests exceeded the latency SLO (p95 > 3.5s)\\n* ~1.8% request failure rate (HTTP 502/503) for EU traffic\\n* No data loss; retries succeeded after mitigation\\n\\nh1. Timeline (UTC)\\n* 10:12 - Alert fired: eu-west request-gateway 5xx > 1%\\n* 10:15 - On-call acknowledged; triage indicates edge-router cache churn\\n* 10:21 - Mitigation 1: disabled new cache key format via feature flag\\n* 10:28 - 5xx decreases but latency still elevated\\n* 10:35 - Mitigation 2: increased redis-edge-cache memory limit + restarted one shard\\n* 10:45 - Latency returns to baseline\\n* 10:59 - Incident resolved; monitoring for recurrence\\n\\nh1. Root cause\\nA configuration rollout introduced a new cache-key schema for routing policy evaluation. In eu-west the cache key cardinality was higher than expected due to a region-specific header normalization discrepancy, causing excessive churn and evictions in redis-edge-cache. Evictions increased cache miss rate, pushing more requests into the slower policy evaluation path and increasing load on request-gateway. Under load, request-gateway emitted intermittent 502/503.\\n\\nh1. Detection\\nDetected via automated alerting on request-gateway 5xx and latency SLO burn for eu-west.\\n\\nh1. What went well\\n* Alerts triggered quickly and were actionable.\\n* Feature flag allowed fast rollback of the risky cache-key change.\\n\\nh1. What went poorly\\n* Canary coverage did not include eu-west header normalization behavior.\\n* Cache churn was not directly monitored; we inferred it from secondary signals.\\n\\nh1. Action items\\n1) Add explicit metric + alert for redis-edge-cache eviction rate and cache miss ratio (Owner: Platform Eng; Due: 2026-02-15)\\n2) Expand routing-policy canary tests to include regional header normalization fixtures (Owner: DevEx; Due: 2026-02-28)\\n3) Update change-management checklist for edge-router config rollouts (Owner: Platform Eng; Due: 2026-02-10)\\n\\nh1. References\\n* Related runbook: oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks/edge-router-triage\\n* Incident channel: #incidents (thread 1770036720)\",\n  \"title_field_name\": \"title\",\n  \"content_field_names\": [\n    \"body\"\n  ],\n  \"dataset_doc_uuid\": \"dsid_140d90d0c1af492a89a8f6e52230ae5d\"\n}",

      "text": "[Document context]\nTitle: Postmortem: EU API latency and elevated 5xx (edge routing cache)\nSource: EnterpriseRAG/confluence\nPath: /knowledge/company/sources/confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/postmortems/2026-01-19-api-eu-degradation.json\nConnector: confluence\nWorkspace: oncall-and-incident-response\n\n##rd * 10 : 45 - latency returns to baseline * 10 : 59 - incident resolved ; monitoring for recurrence h1. root cause a configuration rollout introduced a new cache - key schema for routing policy evaluation. in eu - west the cache key cardinality was higher than expected due to a region - specific header normalization discrepancy, causing excessive churn and evictions in redis - edge - cache. evictions increased cache miss rate, pushing more requests into the slower policy evaluation path and increasing load on request - gateway. under load, request - gateway emitted intermittent 502 / 503. h1. detection detected via automated alerting on request - gateway 5xx and latency slo burn for eu - west.",

document.title: Postmortem: EU API latency and elevated 5xx (edge routing cache)
document.content:
{
  "title": "Postmortem: EU API latency and elevated 5xx (edge routing cache)",
  "space": "oncall-and-incident-response",
  "author": "Ava Chen",
  "owner_team": "engineering",
  "status": "published",
  "created_at": "2026-01-20",
  "last_updated": "2026-02-01",
  "reviewers": [
    "Elliot Price",
    "Jonas Weber"
  ],
  "labels": [
    "postmortem",
    "sev2",
    "customer-impacting",
    "eng-platform",
    "hosted-api",
    "edge-routing"
  ],
  "confidentiality": "internal",
  "body": "h1. Summary
On 2026-01-19 we experienced elevated p95 latency and intermittent HTTP 5xx for a subset of EU-hosted API traffic. The incident lasted 47 minutes end-to-end. Customer impact was concentrated in the eu-west region and primarily affected chat completions with streaming enabled.

*Customer impact:* Yes (degraded performance + partial errors)
*Severity:* SEV-2
*Owning engineering team:* Platform Engineering (Traffic & Edge)
*Primary services:* edge-router, request-gateway, redis-edge-cache

h1. Impact
* ~12% of EU requests exceeded the latency SLO (p95 > 3.5s)
* ~1.8% request failure rate (HTTP 502/503) for EU traffic
* No data loss; retries succeeded after mitigation

h1. Timeline (UTC)
* 10:12 - Alert fired: eu-west request-gateway 5xx > 1%
* 10:15 - On-call acknowledged; triage indicates edge-router cache churn
* 10:21 - Mitigation 1: disabled new cache key format via feature flag
* 10:28 - 5xx decreases but latency still elevated
* 10:35 - Mitigation 2: increased redis-edge-cache memory limit + restarted one shard
* 10:45 - Latency returns to baseline
* 10:59 - Incident resolved; monitoring for recurrence

h1. Root cause
A configuration rollout introduced a new cache-key schema for routing policy evaluation. In eu-west the cache key cardinality was higher than expected due to a region-specific header normalization discrepancy, causing excessive churn and evictions in redis-edge-cache. Evictions increased cache miss rate, pushing more requests into the slower policy evaluation path and increasing load on request-gateway. Under load, request-gateway emitted intermittent 502/503.

h1. Detection
Detected via automated alerting on request-gateway 5xx and latency SLO burn for eu-west.

h1. What went well
* Alerts triggered quickly and were actionable.
* Feature flag allowed fast rollback of the risky cache-key change.

h1. What went poorly
* Canary coverage did not include eu-west header normalization behavior.
* Cache churn was not directly monitored; we inferred it from secondary signals.

h1. Action items
1) Add explicit metric + alert for redis-edge-cache eviction rate and cache miss ratio (Owner: Platform Eng; Due: 2026-02-15)
2) Expand routing-policy canary tests to include regional header normalization fixtures (Owner: DevEx; Due: 2026-02-28)
3) Update change-management checklist for edge-router config rollouts (Owner: Platform Eng; Due: 2026-02-10)

h1. References
* Related runbook: oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks/edge-router-triage
* Incident channel: #incidents (thread 1770036720)",

  "content_field_names": [
    "body"
  ],

}

Read @CLAUDE.md for coding guidelines
# Contributing to LiteLLM

Thank you for your interest in contributing to LiteLLM! We welcome contributions of all kinds - from bug fixes and documentation improvements to new features and integrations.

## **Checklist before submitting a PR**

Here are the core requirements for any PR submitted to LiteLLM:

- [ ] **Sign the Contributor License Agreement (CLA)** - [see details](#contributor-license-agreement-cla)
- [ ] **Keep scope isolated** - Your changes should address 1 specific problem at a time

#### Proxy (Backend) PRs

- [ ] **Add testing** - Adding at least 1 test is a hard requirement - [see details](#adding-testing)
- [ ] **Ensure your PR passes all checks**:
  - [ ] [Unit Tests](#running-unit-tests) - `make test-unit`
  - [ ] [Linting / Formatting](#running-linting-and-formatting-checks) - `make lint`

#### UI PRs

- [ ] **Ensure the UI builds successfully** - `npm run build`
- [ ] **Ensure all UI unit tests pass** - `npm run test`
- [ ] **Add tests for new components or logic** - If you are adding a new component or new logic, add corresponding tests

## **Contributor License Agreement (CLA)**

Before contributing code to LiteLLM, you must sign our [Contributor License Agreement (CLA)](https://cla-assistant.io/BerriAI/litellm). This is a legal requirement for all contributions to be merged into the main repository.

**Important:** We strongly recommend reviewing and signing the CLA before starting work on your contribution to avoid any delays in the PR process.

## Quick Start

### 1. Setup Your Local Development Environment

```bash
# Fork the repository on GitHub (click the Fork button at https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm)
# Then clone your fork locally
git clone https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/litellm.git
cd litellm

# Create a new branch for your feature (see "Commit and Branch Conventions" below)
git checkout -b feature/your-feature

# Install development dependencies
make install-dev

# Install git hooks that enforce commit + branch conventions (one-time, opt-in)
make install-hooks

# Verify your setup works
make help
```

That's it! Your local development environment is ready.

## Commit and Branch Conventions

Commits follow [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) and branches follow [Conventional Branches](https://conventional-branch.github.io/). Run `make install-hooks` once per clone to enable the local git hooks that enforce these — see the [contributor docs](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/extras/contributing_code#commit-and-branch-conventions) for the full type list, examples, the protected-branch bypass list, and how to opt out.

### 2. Development Workflow

Here's the recommended workflow for making changes:

```bash
# Make your changes to the code
# ...

# Format your code (auto-fixes formatting issues)
make format

# Run all linting checks (matches CI exactly)
make lint

# Run unit tests to ensure nothing is broken
make test-unit

# Commit your changes (must follow Conventional Commits — see above)
git add .
git commit -m "feat(scope): your descriptive commit message"

# Push and create a PR (branch must follow Conventional Branches — see above)
git push origin feature/your-feature
```

## Adding Testing

**Adding at least 1 test is a hard requirement for all PRs.**

### Where to Add Tests

Add your tests to the [`tests/test_litellm/` directory](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/tree/main/tests/test_litellm).

- This directory mirrors the structure of the `litellm/` directory
- **Only add mocked tests** - no real LLM API calls in this directory
- For integration tests with real APIs, use the appropriate test directories

### File Naming Convention

The `tests/test_litellm/` directory follows the same structure as `litellm/`:

- `litellm/proxy/caching_routes.py` → `tests/test_litellm/proxy/test_caching_routes.py`
- `litellm/utils.py` → `tests/test_litellm/test_utils.py`

### Example Test

```python
import pytest
from litellm import completion

def test_your_feature():
    """Test your feature with a descriptive docstring."""
    # Arrange
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]
    
    # Act
    # Use mocked responses, not real API calls
    
    # Assert
    assert expected_result == actual_result
```

## Running Tests and Checks

### Running Unit Tests

Run all unit tests (uses parallel execution for speed):

```bash
make test-unit
```

If you're running broader test suites, proxy tests, or anything that touches PostgreSQL-backed fixtures/plugins, install the full local test environment first:

```bash
make install-test-deps
```

This syncs the locked test environment used across the repo, including `psycopg` v3 plus `psycopg-binary` (used by `pytest-postgresql`), `psycopg2-binary` (used by some proxy E2E tests), and a generated Prisma client for DB-backed proxy tests, so pytest startup matches CI without manual package installs.

Run specific test files:
```bash
uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/test_your_file.py -v
```

### Running Linting and Formatting Checks

Run all linting checks (matches CI exactly):

```bash
make lint
```

Individual linting commands:
```bash
make format-check       # Check Black formatting
make lint-ruff          # Run Ruff linting
make lint-basedpyright  # Run basedpyright type checking
make check-circular-imports    # Check for circular imports
make check-import-safety       # Check import safety
```

Apply formatting (auto-fixes issues):
```bash
make format
```

> **Black formatting is enforced in CI.** All PRs must pass the Black formatting check.
>
> - **AI coding agents** (Claude Code, Copilot, Cursor, etc.): `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` instruct agents to run `poetry run black .` before committing.
> - **VS Code users**: Install the [Black Formatter extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=ms-python.black-formatter) and enable format-on-save:
>   ```json
>   {
>     "[python]": {
>       "editor.defaultFormatter": "ms-python.black-formatter",
>       "editor.formatOnSave": true
>     }
>   }
>   ```

### CI Compatibility

To ensure your changes will pass CI, run the exact same checks locally:

```bash
# This runs the same checks as the GitHub workflows
make lint
make test-unit
```

For exact CI compatibility (pins OpenAI version like CI):
```bash
make install-dev-ci     # Installs exact CI dependencies
```

## Available Make Commands

Run `make help` to see all available commands:

```bash
make help                       # Show all available commands
make install-dev               # Install development dependencies
make install-proxy-dev         # Install proxy development dependencies
make install-test-deps         # Install the full local test environment
make format                    # Apply Black code formatting
make format-check              # Check Black formatting (matches CI)
make lint                      # Run all linting checks
make test-unit                 # Run unit tests
make test-integration          # Run integration tests
make test-unit-helm            # Run Helm unit tests
```

## Code Quality Standards

LiteLLM follows the [Google Python Style Guide](https://google.github.io/styleguide/pyguide.html).

Our automated quality checks include:
- **Black** for consistent code formatting
- **Ruff** for linting and code quality
- **basedpyright** for static type checking

import random
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
from typing import TYPE_CHECKING, Any, Dict, List, Optional, Union

import litellm
from litellm import ModelResponse, token_counter, verbose_logger
from litellm.caching.caching import DualCache
from litellm.integrations.custom_logger import CustomLogger
from litellm.litellm_core_utils.core_helpers import safe_divide_seconds
from litellm.litellm_core_utils.core_helpers import _get_parent_otel_span_from_kwargs
from litellm.types.utils import LiteLLMPydanticObjectBase

if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from opentelemetry.trace import Span as _Span

    Span = Union[_Span, Any]
else:
    Span = Any


class RoutingArgs(LiteLLMPydanticObjectBase):
    ttl: float = 1 * 60 * 60  # 1 hour
    lowest_latency_buffer: float = 0
    max_latency_list_size: int = 10


class LowestLatencyLoggingHandler(CustomLogger):
    test_flag: bool = False
    logged_success: int = 0
    logged_failure: int = 0

    def __init__(self, router_cache: DualCache, routing_args: dict = {}):
        self.router_cache = router_cache
        self.routing_args = RoutingArgs(**routing_args)

    def log_success_event(self, kwargs, response_obj, start_time, end_time):
        try:
            """
            Update latency usage on success
            """
            metadata_field = self._select_metadata_field(kwargs)
            if kwargs["litellm_params"].get(metadata_field) is None:

#    This tests the router's handling of zero completion tokens in lowest latency routing

import os
import sys
import time
import pytest

sys.path.insert(
    0, os.path.abspath("../..")
)  # Adds the parent directory to the system path

import litellm
from litellm.caching.caching import DualCache
from litellm.router_strategy.lowest_latency import LowestLatencyLoggingHandler


def test_zero_completion_tokens_no_division_error():
    """
    Test that log_success_event handles zero completion tokens without ZeroDivisionError

    This tests the fix for issue #12641 where responses with zero completion tokens
    (e.g., from Gemini with long contexts) caused ZeroDivisionError
    """
    test_cache = DualCache()

    lowest_latency_logger = LowestLatencyLoggingHandler(router_cache=test_cache)

    deployment_id = "1234"
    kwargs = {
        "litellm_params": {
            "metadata": {
                "model_group": "gemini-2.5-flash",
                "deployment": "gemini/gemini-2.5-flash",
            },
            "model_info": {"id": deployment_id},
        }
    }

    # Create a ModelResponse with zero completion tokens (as reported in issue)
    response_obj = litellm.ModelResponse(
        id="9p13aIGDDNmPmLAP5-23mQQ",
        created=1752669685,
        model="gemini-2.5-flash",
        object="chat.completion",
        choices=[
            litellm.Choices(
                finish_reason="stop",
                index=0,
                message=litellm.Message(
                    content=None, role="assistant", tool_calls=None
                ),
            )
        ],
        usage=litellm.Usage(
            completion_tokens=0,  # This causes the ZeroDivisionError
            prompt_tokens=245537,
            total_tokens=245537,
        ),
    )

    start_time = time.time()
    time.sleep(0.1)  # Simulate some response time
    end_time = time.time()

    # This should not raise ZeroDivisionError
    try:
        lowest_latency_logger.log_success_event(
            response_obj=response_obj,
            kwargs=kwargs,
            start_time=start_time,
            end_time=end_time,
        )
    except ZeroDivisionError:
        pytest.fail(
            "log_success_event raised ZeroDivisionError with zero completion tokens"
        )

    # Verify the deployment was logged (even with zero completion tokens)
    cached_value = test_cache.get_cache(
        key=f"{kwargs['litellm_params']['metadata']['model_group']}_map"
    )
    assert cached_value is not None
    assert deployment_id in cached_value


def test_zero_completion_tokens_with_time_to_first_token():
    """
    Test that time_to_first_token calculation also handles zero completion tokens
    """
    test_cache = DualCache()

    lowest_latency_logger = LowestLatencyLoggingHandler(router_cache=test_cache)

    deployment_id = "1234"
    kwargs = {
        "litellm_params": {
            "metadata": {
                "model_group": "gemini-2.5-flash",
                "deployment": "gemini/gemini-2.5-flash",
            },
            "model_info": {"id": deployment_id},
            "stream": True,
        },
        "completion_start_time": time.time() + 0.05,  # Simulate time to first token
    }

    # Create a ModelResponse with zero completion tokens
    response_obj = litellm.ModelResponse(
        usage=litellm.Usage(
            completion_tokens=0, prompt_tokens=100000, total_tokens=100000
        )
    )

    start_time = time.time()
    time.sleep(0.1)
    end_time = time.time()

    # This should not raise ZeroDivisionError
    try:
        lowest_latency_logger.log_success_event(
            response_obj=response_obj,
            kwargs=kwargs,
            start_time=start_time,

# Latency routing lost-update incident timeline

Issue: LiteLLM #24720
Pinned source: `8f86c87f8e065343af6e74e0823ab8a8276b9528`

## Signature

Two concurrent `async_log_success_event` callbacks for different deployment IDs both read the same `{model_group}_map` snapshot. Each callback adds only its own measurement and writes the entire snapshot. The second whole-map write replaces the first, so the final cache contains one deployment instead of both.

## Deterministic interleaving

1. T+0: callbacks A and B begin for `deployment-a` and `deployment-b`.
2. T+1: the injected cache returns a deep copy of the same empty prior state to A.
3. T+2: the injected cache returns a deep copy of the same empty prior state to B; an event releases both readers only after both reads complete.
4. T+3: A writes a map containing only `deployment-a`.
5. T+4: B writes a map containing only `deployment-b` (or the reverse ordering).
6. T+5: the regression assertion verifies exactly one of the two deployment keys survived.

The event barrier makes the race independent of scheduler timing.

## Operational impact

A missing deployment measurement removes latency evidence used to sort deployments. Repeated loss under concurrent completions can leave the policy without representative measurements and produce selection behavior closer to random choice among otherwise valid deployments.

## Evidence

- Issue snapshot: `/code/upstream-issues/litellm-24720.md` (`enterprise_32709678ecf513e6b78b3e11`)
- Affected code: `/code/litellm/litellm/router_strategy/lowest_latency.py` (`enterprise_a839a3f911067d58bdcc2601`)
- Reproduction: `/code/litellm/tests/test_litellm/test_lowest_latency_zero_tokens.py`
- Concurrency guidance: `/knowledge/company/sources/confluence/architecture-and-standards/coding-standards/concurrency-primitives-and-affinity-guidelines-2026.json` (`dsid_cd133e76dd62456d9182217e280e2cb3`)
- Routing-cache incident precedent: `/knowledge/company/sources/confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/postmortems/2026-01-19-api-eu-degradation.json` (`dsid_140d90d0c1af492a89a8f6e52230ae5d`)

## Reproduction check

Command: `uv run pytest tests/test_litellm/test_lowest_latency_zero_tokens.py -q`

The first execution spent its 120-second window creating the isolated environment and building the local LiteLLM package, so validation is continued after the environment is ready.

"""
Pulls the cost + context window + provider route for known models from https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/blob/main/model_prices_and_context_window.json

This can be disabled by setting the LITELLM_LOCAL_MODEL_COST_MAP environment variable to True.

```
export LITELLM_LOCAL_MODEL_COST_MAP=True
```
"""

import json
import os
from importlib.resources import files
from typing import Dict, List, Optional

import httpx

from litellm import verbose_logger
from litellm.constants import (
    MODEL_COST_MAP_MAX_SHRINK_RATIO,
    MODEL_COST_MAP_MIN_MODEL_COUNT,
)
from litellm.litellm_core_utils.fallback_generalizations import (
    set_fallback_generalizations,
)

FALLBACK_GENERALIZATIONS_KEY = "fallback_generalizations"

# Reserved top-level keys that are not model entries. They must be excluded
# from the model-count integrity check so a real upstream shrink can't be masked.
RESERVED_TOP_LEVEL_KEYS = frozenset({"sample_spec", FALLBACK_GENERALIZATIONS_KEY})


def _count_model_entries(model_cost: dict) -> int:
    """Count actual model entries, excluding reserved meta keys."""
    return sum(1 for key in model_cost if key not in RESERVED_TOP_LEVEL_KEYS)


class GetModelCostMap:
    """
    Handles fetching, validating, and loading the model cost map.

    Only the backup model *count* is cached (a single int). The full
    backup dict is never held in memory — it is only parsed when it
    needs to be *returned* as a fallback.
    """

    _backup_model_count: int = -1  # -1 = not yet loaded

    @staticmethod
    def load_local_model_cost_map() -> dict:
        """Load the local backup model cost map bundled with the package."""
        content = json.loads(
            files("litellm").joinpath("model_prices_and_context_window_backup.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        )
        return content

    @classmethod
    def _get_backup_model_count(cls) -> int:
        """Return the number of models in the local backup (cached int)."""
        if cls._backup_model_count < 0:
            backup = cls.load_local_model_cost_map()
            cls._backup_model_count = _count_model_entries(backup)
        return cls._backup_model_count

    @staticmethod
    def _check_is_valid_dict(fetched_map: dict) -> bool:
        """Check 1: fetched map is a non-empty dict."""
        if not isinstance(fetched_map, dict):
            verbose_logger.warning(
                "LiteLLM: Fetched model cost map is not a dict (type=%s). Falling back to local backup.",
                type(fetched_map).__name__,

            return False

        if len(fetched_map) == 0:
            verbose_logger.warning(
                "LiteLLM: Fetched model cost map is empty. Falling back to local backup.",
            )

# Latency routing concurrency runbook

Owner: SRE / routing
Applies to: LiteLLM lowest-latency routing
Issue: LiteLLM #24720

## Incident signature

Suspect a lost update when concurrent successful completions are recorded for different deployment IDs but the cached `{model_group}_map` contains only a subset of those deployments. The routing symptom is a sudden fall in deployment measurement coverage while request volume remains steady, followed by unexpected randomization or skew among otherwise healthy deployments.

A diagnostic reproduction is definitive when two callbacks read the same prior map, each writes one distinct deployment measurement, and the final map retains only one deployment.

## Detection query

Use the routing telemetry or cache inspection facility available in the environment. Compare distinct successful deployment IDs observed over the last five minutes with IDs present in the latency map:

```text
success_ids = distinct(deployment_id where callback=success and model_group=$MODEL_GROUP over 5m)
latency_ids = keys(cache[$MODEL_GROUP + "_map"])
missing_ids = success_ids - latency_ids
alert when count(success_ids) >= 2 and count(missing_ids) > 0
```

Corroborate with rising lowest-latency selection variance or traffic skew while health, capacity, and provider errors are stable. Do not treat cache eviction alone as proof; TTL expiry and normal sample expiration must be excluded.

## Immediate mitigation

1. Reduce callback concurrency for the affected router instance if operationally safe.
2. Temporarily select a deterministic routing policy or pin healthy deployments while retaining capacity headroom.
3. Preserve the affected map and five minutes of callback/deployment telemetry for comparison.
4. Roll out the handler-scoped serialization fix to a canary.

Do not place a process-wide lock around provider requests or other network I/O.

## Permanent mitigation

Serialize the async latency-map read–modify–write inside each `LowestLatencyLoggingHandler` instance. The critical section must begin immediately before the local cache read and end immediately after the cache write. Keep provider request execution and unrelated handlers outside it. Preserve the existing TTL, maximum sample-list size, latency/TTFT calculations, TPM/RPM buckets, and selection/expiration behavior.

## Validation

1. Run the deterministic concurrent regression test. Both `deployment-a` and `deployment-b` must remain in `latency-race_map`.
2. Run existing lowest-latency tests, especially zero-token, streaming TTFT, sample-window, selection-buffer, and expiration cases.
3. Verify formatting, linting, and Python compilation for changed files.
4. Canary with at least two concurrently active deployments. Confirm `missing_ids` remains empty and compare p95/p99 routing latency and traffic distribution with baseline.
5. Confirm no lock spans provider calls; only cache update work may be serialized within one handler.

## Rollback

Revert the scoped serialization change and switch the canary to the prior artifact. Until a corrected build is ready, use the immediate mitigation above. After rollback, verify router callback throughput, cache-map coverage, traffic distribution, and latency SLOs. Retain the regression test and incident evidence even if the implementation is rolled back.

## Evidence

- `/code/upstream-issues/litellm-24720.md` (`enterprise_32709678ecf513e6b78b3e11`)
- `/code/litellm/litellm/router_strategy/lowest_latency.py` (`enterprise_a839a3f911067d58bdcc2601`)
- `/code/litellm/tests/test_litellm/test_lowest_latency_zero_tokens.py`
